title: Add slot succession sequencer and thermal-aware slew controller for stable burst injection
author: Ravi Patel
description:
Motivation: During a set of production-mirroring benchmark runs we observed repeated short-lived p95/p99 spikes correlated with tight slot contention and abrupt GPU thermal headroom reductions. These microbursts caused transient QoS violations in the scheduler and produced noisy latency tails in our profiling baselines. This PR introduces two coordinated components to make burst injection more predictable in the bench environment: (1) a slot succession sequencer that coalesces and sequences concurrent slot grants to avoid pathological overlap patterns, and (2) a thermal-aware slew controller that adaptively paces mini-batches when telemetry indicates thermal headroom pressure.

Scope: Changes are confined to the benchmark-lab harness and its synthetic workload runners; no production runtime code is modified. Key pieces: a deterministic sequencer implemented in Go (benchmarks/slot_sequencer), a lightweight thermal predictor in Python that consumes telemetry samples and produces a short-term headroom estimate, and a controller that gates burst submission. We also add telemetry exporters and tagging to make post-run attribution easier.

What this does:
- Implements a slot succession algorithm that enforces a soft inter-slot spacing policy based on observed kernel durations and token/sequence length distribution.
- Adds a thermal headroom estimator that smooths temperature/clock samples and exposes a headroom score (0..1) used by the slew controller.
- Introduces a slew controller that throttles mini-batch submit rates when headroom < threshold, with configurable aggressive/recovery modes.
- Exposes new metrics: bench_slot_latency_ms, bench_slot_overlap_count, bench_thermal_headroom (gauge), bench_slew_throttle_ratio.
- Includes a new deterministic workload playbook (sample_playbooks/slot_succession.yaml) to reproduce the scenario and a docs page with reproduction steps.

Benchmarks & results: Microbench runs against the 2026-01-30 baseline show: median latency unchanged, p95 improved by ~12-18% under high-concurrency bursts, p99 tail reduced by 20-35% in the synthetic token-surge scenario, and GPU thermal oscillation amplitude reduced by ~40%. These runs are attached in the CI bench-regression artifacts.

Testing & QA: Unit tests for sequencer logic and predictor added. Integration harness that runs the playbook for short and long durations (5m/1h) included. I ran the integration suite on an m6 GPU instance matrix. Checklist: 
- [x] Unit tests added and passing locally
- [x] Integration playbook validated on staging cluster
- [x] Bench regression run (baseline comparison) attached to CI
- [x] Docs page draft added under docs/benchmarks
- [x] Performance dashboards updated with new metric mappings

Backward compatibility & safety: Default knobs are conservative: sequencer disabled by default in existing playbooks unless the new playbook is used; slew controller is opt-in via config. No breaking changes to existing harness APIs.

How to run locally: 
1) cd benchmarks/slot_sequencer
2) go build && ./slot_sequencer --playbook ../../benchmarks/config/sample_playbooks/slot_succession.yaml
3) tail -f /tmp/bench-telemetry.log or use the provided exporter to push to prometheus for dashboarding.

Related: ENG-4823 (investigate thermal-driven latency tails), ENG-4890 (stability work for synthetic surges), SUP-9123 (customer incident that motivated conservative pacing).

Notes: This PR purposefully keeps the control logic in the benchmark harness (not in the serving runtime) so we can iterate on policies quickly. If we see robust improvement across more workloads we will propose a follow-up RFC to upstream a vetted policy into the runtime's admission layer.

release_notes: Introduce slot succession sequencer and thermal-aware slew controller in the benchmark harness to reduce p95/p99 spikes during synthetic token surges. Opt-in via new playbook; non-breaking.
summary: Bench harness additions to sequence slot grants and adaptively throttle bursts based on thermal headroom; reduces latency tail noise in synthetic surge scenarios and adds observability for root cause analysis.
